answer: A child can sign up to an online service on their own without a parent agreeing to the use of their data if they are at least 16 years old. Member States may provide for a lower age not below 13 years, but this must be provided by law.

The controller should be obliged to respond to requests from the data subject without undue delay and at the latest within one month. The period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests. The controller shall inform the data subject of any such extension within one month of receipt of the request, together with the reasons for the delay.
The controller should notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it.

The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time. The withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal. Prior to giving consent, the data subject shall be informed thereof. It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.

Data that has been truly anonymised is not necessarily covered by the GDPR. According to Article 67, personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation and could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered as information on an identifiable natural person. This implies that even after anonymization, if there's still a risk of re-identification, it may not fully comply with GDPR requirements. However, Article 68(1), point (c) specifically provides for certain categories of electronic health data to remain sensitive and non-personal in anonymized format.

Yes, a business can rely on its legitimate interest when it uses customer data to send marketing, as stated in the passages. The processing of personal data for direct marketing purposes may be regarded as carried out for a legitimate interest. However, the right to object to such processing should also be explicitly brought to the attention of the data subject at any time and free of charge.

The designation of a data protection officer is required in cases where:

1. The processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity.
2. The core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, scope and purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or
3. The core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of personal data pursuant to Article 9 and personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10.

In these cases, a single data protection officer may be designated for several such authorities or bodies, taking account of their organisational structure and size.

Yes, a company that watches a busy public square with cameras on a big scale has to do an impact assessment first. This is indicated in the passages where it states that impact assessment is required for monitoring publicly accessible areas on a large scale, especially when using optic-electronic devices or for any other operations where the competent supervisory authority considers that the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects.

You can file a complaint with a supervisory authority, in particular in the Member State of your habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement. If you consider that the processing of your personal data is infringing this Regulation, you should lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. The supervisory authority will inform you on the progress and outcome of the complaint including the possibility of a judicial remedy pursuant to Article 78.

The Board is composed of the head of one supervisory authority of each Member State and of the European Data Protection Supervisor, or their respective representatives.

The EHDS regulation is meant to improve the functioning of the internal market by laying down a uniform legal and technical framework for electronic health record systems in conformity with Union values. It will be a key element in creating a strong and resilient European Health Union.

After a hospital visit, you should have immediate access to your personal electronic health data through an electronic health data access service. There are no specific mentions of charges for accessing these records; however, fees may apply for secondary use as per Article 62.

Article 4 states that natural persons or their representatives shall have the right to download free of charge an electronic version of their personal electronic health data immediately after it has been registered in an EHR system. Article 9 also mentions that you should have the right to obtain information, including through automatic notifications, on any access to your personal electronic health data.

Regarding charges, Article 5 states that health data access bodies may charge fees for making electronic health data available for secondary use, but these fees shall be in proportion to the cost of making the data available and not restrict competition.

The priority categories of personal electronic health data for electronic exchange include patient summaries, electronic prescriptions, electronic dispensations, medical imaging studies and related imaging reports, and medical test results such as laboratory results and related reports.

Yes, you can prevent certain doctors from viewing parts of your electronic health file by restricting access as referred to in Article 8. Natural persons have the right to restrict the access of health professionals and healthcare providers to all or parts of their personal electronic health data.

Yes, according to passage 4, using electronic health data for advertising or marketing activities is prohibited. Therefore, companies cannot use health data obtained through the EHDS for such purposes.

Yes, health records can be reused under the EHDS to monitor threats to public health as specified in Article 7(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/868, which entrusts health data access bodies with powers to take decisions on access to and secondary use of health data. This could include monitoring Union policies on a regular basis through such data access, which may be required by specific Member States or throughout the whole territory of the Union.

Yes, you can request the rectification of your personal electronic health data online through an electronic health data access service. The rectification requests should be treated by the relevant controllers in line with Regulation (EU) 2016/679, if necessary involving health professionals. This correction is immediate and free of charge.

Yes, researchers need to pay for getting health data under the EHDS. The fees must be in proportion to the cost of making the data available and they cannot restrict competition. There is no explicit limit mentioned on what can be charged, but transparency and non-discrimination are required according to Article 6 from Regulation (EU) 2022/868.

Chapter IV applies from 26 March 2029, and it is mentioned that Chapter III applies from 26 March 2031. However, the general application date for EHDS is not specified directly in the given passages. Therefore, no specific date can be determined based on the provided information.

Yes, if a fitness app (wellness application) claims interoperability with an EHR system, it needs to be accompanied by a label clearly indicating its compliance with the common specifications and essential requirements laid down in Annex II.

Yes, the patient summary includes information about your vaccinations as it is part of significant clinical facts related to an identified natural person and essential for safe and efficient healthcare.

Article 71(4) of the GDPR is pointed to for the services doctors use to access patient records in the EHDS.

Pseudonymization means processing personal data in such a way that the individual is not directly or indirectly identified. In the GDPR, pseudonymization can be used for statistical or research purposes.

According to Article 67 of the EHDS document, health data access bodies should provide access to electronic health data in pseudonymised format unless they intend to bring datasets already held by them into an anonymised format as per Article 68(1), point (c). In such cases, anonymized data must be provided. Therefore, EHDS must provide anonymised rather than pseudonymised data when the processing cannot be carried out using anonymised data.

If you have opted out of the EHDS access services, your data cannot be used for secondary use under this Regulation. However, it is possible to access the data generated during the period of the opt-out in emergency situations, provided that the processing does not violate the right to protect vital interests as referred to in Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

No, the passage provided does not contain specific information about what happens after a company deletes your data and informs you. The passages focus on conditions for transferring personal data, data access by health data access bodies, and obligations regarding erasure of personal data. There is no mention of notifying other organizations that have shared the data upon deletion request.

When an online service collects data from children, specific protection should apply. This includes using consent of the holder of parental responsibility and ensuring transparency about personal data collection. Consent is not necessary in the context of preventive or counselling services offered directly to a child.

Article 54 states that Health Data Users shall only process electronic health data for secondary use on the basis of and in accordance with the purposes contained in a data permit issued pursuant to Article 68, health data requests approved pursuant to Article 69 or, in situations referred to in Article 67(3), an access approval from the relevant authorised participant in HealthData@EU referred to in Article 75. This implies that patients can refuse their health data being used for secondary use as it requires a permit or approval.

However, there is no passage explicitly stating whether patients have the right to refuse both access services and research reuse of their health data. The passages focus more on the processing and usage conditions rather than patient rights regarding refusal. Therefore, based solely on the provided information, we cannot definitively answer if patients can refuse both types of uses.
